From basic virtualization to production-grade virtual machines, this chapter covers modern UEFI/TPM firmware support, VFIO hardware passthrough, virtio paravirtualized driver optimization, virtiofs file sharing, and advanced disk-image operations.
1. UEFI firmware and TPM: modern OS support
Choose firmware based on guest and boot requirements. SeaBIOS remains usable for supported legacy guests, while UEFI provides a modern firmware interface:
Do not confuse MBR addressing limits with BIOS; BIOS can boot GPT disks with a suitable bootloader
Shorter total boot time is not guaranteed
Traditional bootloaders can manage multiple operating systems, but lack the UEFI boot-entry interface
UEFI boot manager with multiple entries

The filenames and directories below are distribution-specific examples. CODE/VARS sizes, architecture, and Secure Boot keys must match; check domcapabilities and firmware metadata first. New domains can use automatic firmware selection. An existing domain's NVRAM contains boot entries and keys, so do not casually delete or recreate it just to move paths.
OVMF is a UEFI firmware implementation built from Tianocore EDK2 for QEMU/KVM.

Each virtual machine needs its own NVRAM file OVMF_VARS.fd is a template; libvirt copies it to /var/lib/libvirt/qemu/nvram/ when creating a virtual machine. VMs must not share a VARS file, or they will overwrite one another's boot entries and certificates.
In Secure Boot mode, OVMF verifies bootloader signatures. Linux distributions usually include signed bootloaders (shim + GRUB), and Windows also supports this natively.

Secure Boot conflicts with some GPU ROMs
With both Secure Boot and GPU passthrough enabled, a GPU's Video ROM may fail to load because signature verification fails. First check the firmware, ROM type, signatures, and guest logs, then decide whether to use a verified ROM or adjust policy. Disabling Secure Boot is not the default fix and may also trigger disk-encryption recovery.

Windows 11 officially requires TPM 2.0. SWTPM is a common emulated implementation, but a compliant hardware TPM backend can also be used. Check the full requirements as well, including CPU, memory, storage, UEFI, and Secure Boot capability.

Persisting TPM state The TPM emulator stores its state under /var/lib/libvirt/swtpm/<vm-uuid>/. If TPM-dependent full-disk encryption such as BitLocker is enabled, backing up this directory is critical: losing the TPM state means the disk cannot be decrypted.

The VFIO/IOMMU group is the unit of isolation. Before passthrough, check every device in the group, host dependencies, and a recovery control path. ID-based binding may match multiple devices of the same model, and blacklisting may disable all of the host's GPUs. ACS override is a dangerous software method of splitting groups available in some patched kernels; it does not create hardware DMA isolation and is not a default step.

VFIO (Virtual Function I/O) directly assigns physical PCIe devices to virtual machines for near-bare-metal I/O performance. Typical uses include GPU passthrough for gaming/rendering/AI training, NVMe passthrough for databases, and USB controller passthrough for latency-sensitive peripherals.
The IOMMU (Input-Output Memory Management Unit) is the hardware foundation of VFIO, responsible for mapping DMA addresses into the virtual machine's address space.

IOMMU groups determine which devices can be passed through independently. VFIO requires all relevant devices in a group to meet safe binding conditions, such as being bound to VFIO or unbound from their host driver. This does not mean every function must be exposed to the same guest. Devices in the same group that are still used by the host must not compromise isolation.

Security risks of the ACS patch If a GPU shares an IOMMU group with other devices, such as a USB controller, NVMe drive, or NIC, the pcie_acs_override=downstream,multifunction kernel parameter can forcibly split the group. However, this breaks hardware isolation: devices in the same group can access one another through DMA. It must not be an automatic fallback after moving slots fails. If reliable isolation is unavailable, abandon the assignment or replace the hardware.

For a gaming VM, pass through a dedicated USB 3.0 PCIe expansion card. This lets you physically switch peripherals such as the keyboard, mouse, and headset.

SMT / Hyper-Threading considerations The cpuset numbers are illustrative logical CPU IDs; 2 and 8 are not guaranteed to be SMT siblings. When should you use HugePages?
For virtual machines with memory > 8GB that need stable performance, such as gaming, databases, and AI inference, huge pages can significantly reduce TLB misses. For lightweight VMs, however, THP (Transparent Huge Pages) is sufficient.

4. virtiofs: file sharing between host and virtual machine
virtiofs is a paravirtualized filesystem introduced in QEMU 5.0+ that replaces the aging virtio-9p and provides high-performance file sharing between host and guest.

qemu-img is intended for offline disks. Stop all users of a disk and take backups before any modification, conversion, repair, snapshot, resize, commit, or rebase; even online queries may see inconsistent metadata. check -r all can lose data, so copy the original first. qemu-img internal disk snapshots do not save guest RAM, UEFI NVRAM, or TPM state.
qcow2 supports incremental layers based on a backing file, similar to an overlay filesystem:

Dangerous backing-chain operations
Sectors in the base that are not overridden by the overlay are still read, so rewriting a shared base changes the data view of every guest that depends on it. This should not be interpreted as "sector offsets necessarily become invalid." The base should remain immutable during normal operation.
Before making changes, list all dependent chains, stop all writers, and back up the entire chain.
commit writes to the backing file and may affect other overlays; it is not a generally safe preparatory step before modifying a shared base.
Safe-mode rebase reads the old and new bases while preserving the guest's view. -u changes only metadata, and misuse can corrupt that view. Check the formats, paths, and underlying data.
When you need an independent copy, prefer using convert to flatten the offline chain, then verify the copy. Do not run these tools on online images.

Before defining an LVM/disk pool, check the device's stable ID, capacity, existing partitions, and users. Defining a pool is different from building/formatting it; the latter may destroy existing data. A physical block device is not a "blank image," so do not act on a /dev/sdX name alone. The security and performance of NAT, isolated, bridge, and macvtap depend on rules, topology, and workload. The high/low ratings in the table are only an overview from the original notes, not measured results. NAT/isolated do not block guests from accessing the host bridge or other guests on the same subnet. bridge/macvtap require authorization from the external network, and macvtap is not PCI passthrough. Ordinary Wi-Fi clients often cannot transparently bridge multiple MAC addresses. Prepare local or out-of-band recovery before changing the host IP or routes.
High performance on a single host
macvtap associates a guest virtual NIC with a host physical interface without a traditional bridge. It still traverses the host networking path and is not PCI/VFIO NIC passthrough:
Traffic between VMs is forwarded through an external switch
VMs on the host can communicate directly
Multiple VMs on a single host
VMs are completely isolated from one another
One VM has exclusive use of the NIC
High performance for a single VM

macvtap limitations
In macvtap bridge mode, the host itself cannot communicate with its VMs, even on the same physical NIC. This is a design limitation of Linux macvlan. If host-to-VM communication is required, configure an additional macvlan on the host's macvtap interface or use a traditional bridge instead.
